prompt.context: Our client is a private equity firm looking to acquire Funeral Co, a company operating 100 funeral homes in the US. The client targets to grow Funeral Co's EBITDA by 15% annually over five years.
prompt.question: Should the client acquire Funeral Co?

clarifying_info.q: What types of services does Funeral Co currently offer?
clarifying_info.a: The target is currently offering only burial services, serving mainly Christians in small towns.

The funeral homes industry is highly fragmented with over 20,000 funeral homes in the US. 75-80% are owned by individuals or families; ~20-25% operated by private corporations. Funeral Co is the only funeral home in the areas it operates in.
There are 2 types of funeral ceremonies: burial and cremation. Industry trend is shifting towards more cremation.

clarifying_info.q: What is the cost structure like?
clarifying_info.a: Funeral homes have a high fixed cost structure.

clarifying_info.q: What does the PE firm want to focus on?
clarifying_info.a: The client wants to concentrate on increasing EBITDA only — specifically to double EBITDA in 5 years (15% IRR over 5 years roughly equals 2x).

exhibits.title: Consumer Survey
exhibits.shows: A consumer survey showing customer preferences for burial vs. cremation services, indicating the current offering (burial with services only) and a potential new offering (cremation with services in existing funeral homes).
exhibits.data: Survey data comparing customer demand for burial-with-services versus cremation-with-services; highlights that a segment of customers currently travel to neighboring towns or do basic cremations at home because cremation is unavailable locally.

framework: 1. Financial (EBITDA) — Revenue: price per burial, burials per year, number of locations; Costs: fixed (SG&A, rent) and variable (fuel, chemicals/formaldehyde)
2. Funeral Home Market — Competitors: fragmentation/consolidation, service differentiation; Customers: changing preferences, segmentation by WTP; Growth: aging community demographics
3. Opportunities to expand product offerings — Burial vs. cremation; Value-added services

questions.prompt: The target is currently offering only burial services with $6,000 revenue earned per burial at 20% EBITDA margin. How much EBITDA can the burial services segment generate in the 5th year, and how much extra EBITDA does Funeral Co need to generate outside burial services by the end of the PE firm's 5-year holding period?
questions.guidance: Candidate should (1) calculate current revenue and EBITDA, (2) project burial segment EBITDA to Year 5 using given growth rates, (3) compute the target EBITDA needed for 2x, and (4) identify the gap that must be closed by other means.

math.setup: Current: 100 locations × 150 burials/year × $6,000/burial = $90M revenue; EBITDA = 20% × $90M = $18M. Target EBITDA = $18M × 2 = $36M. Year-5 burial revenue: volume +3%/yr and price +2%/yr over 5 years ≈ combined ~5% per year compounded. Revenue ≈ $90M × (1.03)^5 × (1.02)^5 ≈ $90M × 1.159 × 1.104 ≈ ~$115M. EBITDA at 20% margin ≈ $23M.
math.answer: Burial services can organically generate ~$23M EBITDA by Year 5; Funeral Co needs an additional $13M EBITDA from other sources.

questions.prompt: The target is wondering if they should introduce cremation services in existing funeral homes. Revenue per cremation is 33% lower than burial services. Does customer demand support this? Does the target have the capability? Is it profitable, and can cremation alone bridge the $13M EBITDA gap?
questions.guidance: Candidate should use Exhibit 1 to confirm demand supports cremation. Then assess capability (one extra employee per location, no interior changes). Then calculate cremation EBITDA and check if it closes the gap.

math.setup: Price per cremation = $4,000 (33% below $6,000). Gross profit margin = 70% → GP per cremation = $2,800. Volume = 50 cremations/year/location × 100 locations = 5,000 cremations. No incremental SG&A. EBITDA = GP (since no extra SG&A).
steps: $14M > $13M gap → cremation alone bridges the entire gap
math.answer: Cremation adds $14M in EBITDA, which exceeds the $13M gap. Yes, cremation alone can bridge the shortfall.

questions.prompt: What else can Funeral Co do to bridge the EBITDA gap (or grow beyond it)?
questions.guidance: Candidate should brainstorm both revenue and cost levers. Strong answers distinguish between viable options and those constrained by zoning, pricing laws, or fund horizon. Bonus if candidate identifies why certain obvious options (acquisitions, new locations, aggressive price hikes) are not feasible.

brainstorming.prompt: What else can Funeral Co do to bridge the EBITDA gap?

categories.name: New Revenue Streams (Viable)
ideas: Offer direct cremation (lower-cost, leverages existing employees, adds $3–4M EBITDA in steady state from Year 3+)
Pre-need sales — contract funeral arrangements before death, in partnership with lawyers or life insurance firms
Expand customer base to non-Christian communities (currently serve only Christians)
Increase value-added services bundled with existing offerings

categories.name: Cost Reduction (Viable)
ideas: Hire labor on contractual basis to address ~130 days of idle time (even post-cremation ~80 days idle); potential savings of $4–5M/year, though quality of service risk exists

categories.name: Not Feasible (good insight if raised)
ideas: Acquire more funeral homes — strict zoning laws prohibit sale in most areas; other players unwilling to sell
Open new funeral home locations — takes many years to build and ramp up, outside PE fund's 5-year horizon
Increase pricing for burial/cremation — pricing laws prohibit abnormal price increases

recommendation: Yes, the client should acquire Funeral Co

The $13M EBITDA gap can be closed — primarily by introducing cremation services in existing funeral homes, which adds ~$14M in EBITDA with low incremental investment (one additional employee per location, no structural changes)
risks: Target may not be able to reskill existing employees for cremation services and may need to hire more staff
Christian customers may object to burials and cremations being co-located in the same funeral home
Management bandwidth will be stretched if the company offers different service types simultaneously
next_steps: Survey families who typically choose burials to gauge comfort with cremations being offered at the same location
Conduct full due diligence on Funeral Co's operations, financials, and workforce capabilities
Discuss and agree on acquisition valuation with the PE firm
